11931-the-mystery-of-monastery-farm:
Naylor's 1908 mystery opens with a great bank robbery. On April 11, officers of the Bank of England learn of a special meeting called for ten at night, and fifteen directors take their usual places. From that dramatic start the story winds toward Monastery Farm, where a ledger's handwriting catches a bishop's eye.

The bishop remarks that he has seen such fine work only once before, in the writing of his own dear boy. Later scenes follow bishops strolling across a park, a doctor visiting a patient named Carl, and quiet interviews in an office. Naylor builds suspense from documents, resemblances, and guarded conversations rather than from chases alone.
12021-adopting-an-abandoned-farm:
Kate Sanborn's 1891 book Adopting an Abandoned Farm moves from Gotham to Gooseville, through auctions, buying a horse, pets. Starting a poultry farm, to ghosts, daily distractions, and the prose of New England farm life. Later chapters record the passing of the peacocks and a backward look, with an epigraph on an old farm-house with meadows wide and sweet with clover.

Sanborn, a lecturer and writer, tells how a city woman took up a derelict farm and learned its work, animals, and neighbors. The book's humor lies in the gap between romantic ideas of country life and its daily prose. Its charm in Sanborn's willingness to laugh at herself while she learns.
13347-wildflowers-of-the-farm:
Arthur O. Cooke's country-life reader walks young readers round Willow Farm and its lanes, coppices, walls, hayfields, and cornfields. It starts at a gravel drive, a white gate, and a great mulberry tree. It then names the flowers and weeds found in each place, from violets and almond blossom to clover and cornfield plants.

Cooke explains what each plant is for, not only what it looks like. Traveller's Joy climbs the hedge, dead nettles mimic true nettles, hemp gives string and rope, and meadow foxtail and cocksfoot make good grazing sward. The book teaches farm botany by place and season, with pictures to help a child match name to flower in the field.
13885-echoes-from-the-sabine-farm:
Roswell Martin Field and Eugene Field published Echoes from the Sabine Farm in 1899. The brothers freely paraphrased odes of Horace into English verse and prose. They had earlier printed small books of verse and tales at Chicago. A sponsor urged Field to make a book from the Horace pieces he had on hand.

Paraphrases include odes to Lydia, to Quintius Hirpinus, and to a jar of wine. Wine, women, and song, fortune, and Pompeius Varus also appear. The Fields keep Horace's ease and wit rather than strict literal sense. The book suits readers who enjoy classical poetry in friendly dress. It also shows American literary life at the century's end.
1441-the-story-of-an-african-farm:
Olive Schreiner's first novel, first signed Ralph Iron, is set on a lonely Karoo farm in South Africa. Three children grow up there: Lyndall, fierce and questioning; Waldo, dreamy and earnest; and Em, quiet and kind, all watched over by a harsh German overseer and his scheming wife.

Through childhood scenes, a false preacher, and adult choices about love, work, and faith, the novel asks what freedom means for women and for thinking minds in a hard land. Its structure is loose but its feeling is strong. It is a landmark of South African writing and of feminist fiction.
14897-that-old-time-child-roberta-her-ho:
Sophie Fox Sea's 1892 book follows Roberta, an old-time child, through home life on a farm, printed in Louisville and dedicated to Mrs. Preston Pope. An illustration shows a child asking must I look so when I die, with a nurse's answer about dreadful men who said boo.

Farm days, family, servants and small terrors shape Roberta's world, told in a voice that recalls a Kentucky childhood with affection. Sea writes for readers who remember, or want to know, a farm household before modern change: work, play, church and the stories adults told children at night. The book is local colour and memoir in story form, warm and unhurried.
15029-kit-of-greenacre-farm:
Izola Forrester's 1919 girls' story centers on Kit, a lively young heroine guarding her family's huckleberry patch at Greenacre Farm. From a cupola lookout she watches for raiders, since a bumper berry crop draws pickers from towns miles away. Friends, a hired man named Shad, and farm neighbors fill her days.

Through thirty chapters Kit faces trespassers, family counsels, a mummy exhibit, and hopes for paying guests, learning pluck and good sense along the way. The tone is sunny and old-fashioned, with country detail at every turn. Young readers, and nostalgic older ones, will enjoy its outdoor fun and warm family feeling.
16369-fishing-with-a-worm:
Bliss Perry defends the humble worm against the snobbery of fly fishermen in this 1916 book of essays. He opens with Izaak Walton's line about his last fish, then admits the fisherman's happy inconsistency: he watches wind when he should sow, and clouds when he should reap. A red-bearded carpenter who leaves good work to fish sets the tone.

Perry writes with humor and ease, praising lazy days by the water over busy virtue. The essays wander from boyhood memories to the philosophy of sport. Anglers and idlers alike will enjoy a book that treats fishing as rest, reflection, and quiet rebellion against the clock.
16525-the-fat-of-the-land-the-story-of-a:
John Williams Streeter tells how he and Polly made an American farm in this 1904 Macmillan book, reprinted three times in its first months. Chapters run from hunting for land and boring for water to taking possession, platting the farm, fencing, and building. Trees, hens, White Wyandottes, pork, and the old orchard fill the practical middle.

Streeter writes with humor and hard-won sense, treating farming as both business and joy. Polly's judgment hall gets its own chapter, a sign of the book's domestic warmth. Readers who dream of land will find a cheerful, detailed account of starting a farm from scratch.
1711-child-of-storm:
Mameena is a Zulu woman of striking beauty and will, and her choices set chiefs against each other in the years before the Zulu war. Quatermain hears of her through Zikali the wizard, watches her marriage gifts and ambushes unfold, and finds himself drawn into a struggle over who will follow King Panda.

The story weighs Umbelazi against Cetewayo as Panda's heir, and it follows Saduko, Mameena's husband, through loyalty and revenge. Haggard writes the Zulu kingdom from inside its politics rather than from outside its battles, and Mameena herself — proud, clever, and doomed — carries the book.
17861-the-wrack-of-the-storm:
Maurice Maeterlinck wrote The Wrack of the Storm as a set of war essays, printed with his other works in a London edition. Maeterlinck, the Belgian Nobel laureate famed for The Blue Bird and The Life of the Bee, turned his pen to Belgium's fate in the Great War.

Essays run from After the Victory to King Albert, the hostage cities, the drive to save four cities, and two pieces pro patria, on heroism and home. Maeterlinck writes with grief, pride, and moral fire for his invaded land. The book gives a poet's war-time voice, and a moving Belgian view of 1914 and its wreck.
19555-bunny-brown-and-his-sister-sue-on-:
Laura Lee Hope wrote this tale of Bunny Brown and his sister Sue on Grandpa's farm, issued in New York in the mid nineteen teens with pictures by Florence England Nosworthy. Farm days bring animals, brooks, and small mischief in the series' gentle style.

One scene has Bunny damming a brook into a waterfall, to the surprise of a neighbor whose chicken yard runs dry, while Sue, as always, tells everything. The book charms by its simple pleasures: water, mud, and children learning to set things right. Chapters promise a runaway monkey, a queer slide, and a lost horse among the farm's small excitements.
19655-kitchener-s-mob-adventures-of-an-a:
In August 1914, London walls filled with calls for volunteers for the Great War. The seasoned regulars nicknamed the new mass army Kitchener's Mob, after Lord Kitchener. At first only some sixty thousand men stood under arms. Millions more were still to come. Kitchener's Mob tells the adventures of an American serving in that British army.

Volunteer armies run on spirit before they gain skill. An American voice inside the ranks gives the story an outsider's edge. Readers follow the shift from civilian crowds to soldiers at war. Books like this fed home-front hunger for the front. They remain useful records of how the first mass armies of 1914 felt to join.
20446-america-for-americans-the-typical-:
America for Americans is a Thanksgiving sermon arguing for stricter limits on immigration and naturalization. The preacher treats the subject as one of deep national feeling. He says intelligent foreigners approve his course.

He cites a memorial sent to Congress by the Germans of Wisconsin. They asked for changes in the naturalization laws, and he uses their plea as support. The sermon shows a strand of nineteenth-century preaching that tied gratitude for the nation to guarding its gates. It also preserves the exact terms in which that case was made from the pulpit.
21937-modern-icelandic-plays-eyvind-of-t:
Two plays by Jóhann Sigurjónsson bring modern Icelandic drama to English readers in this 1916 volume of Scandinavian Classics. Henninge Krohn Schanche translated both for the American-Scandinavian Foundation. Eyvind of the Hills tells of an outlaw of the Icelandic highlands, a figure from old saga country. The Hraun Farm turns to the lava-field farms where families held hard ground against a harder climate.

The Foundation published the series hoping Americans would know the North's great literature better. Sigurjónsson was Iceland's leading modern dramatist, writing in both Icelandic and Danish. His people speak sparely and carry saga-sized fates. These translations, careful and plain, let English readers meet a literature most had never seen. The hills and lava farms of Iceland stand behind every line.
23000-orley-farm:
Anthony Trollope lists the road ahead in Orley Farm's chapter headings. John Kenneby goes to Hamworth. John Kenneby's courtship follows. Then come Lady Mason's nobility, Orme's weakness, a woman's idea of friendship, and the Angel of Light under a cloud. The headings alone sketch a crowded, moral world.

At the center stands Lady Mason of Orley Farm, accused of forging a codicil to keep the estate for her son. Trollope builds his long novel from law, gossip, and conscience, county families circling a single disputed signature. Serialized with illustrations in 1861 and 1862, it became one of his most admired works. Readers who settle into its pace get Trollope at full power, patient, funny, and unsparing.
23832-summerfield-or-life-on-a-farm:
Day Kellogg Lee published Summerfield, or Life on a Farm, at Auburn in 1852, dedicating it to his venerated father, a pioneer of the lake country. The introduction states its aim plainly: fiction should serve morality and religion, and Lee's tale teaches a lesson of the utmost practical importance for everyday life.

That lesson is contentment with a useful and productive occupation. The best compost for the lands, Herrick's epigraph says, is the wise master's feet and hands. Lee's farm story follows that wisdom through seasons of work, showing that honest labor, well directed, brings peace and honor in the autumn of life. It is a moral tale in the manner of its age.
23943-the-chickens-of-fowl-farm:
Lena E. Barksdale published The Chickens of Fowl Farm in Philadelphia in 1898, with Kodak illustrations by the author herself. Her preface is dated August 22, 1898, and notes that the little chicken book was finished on her eleventh birthday. Most of the chickens she writes of are members of her own family, so she knows them well.

Uncle Remus already spoke for other creatures, and horses through Black Beauty, Barksdale writes. Now she wishes to give the chickens a chance. The book opens with a talk in the chickenyard, where young Scratchfoot complains of summer talk, and Uncle Red Nose Mike poses a riddle about the cravat Mr. Hog would choose. It is a child's barnyard comedy, told from inside the flock.
25051-space-platform:
Murray Leinster's Space Platform, first published by Shasta and reissued by Pocket Books in 1953, is an early novel about building humanity's first station in orbit. Young engineer Joe Kenmore travels to the Bootstrap launch site to fit pilot gyros to the Platform, expecting hard technical work.

Sabotage soon threatens the project, and Joe finds himself hunting agents willing to kill to wreck it. Alongside a rugged steelworker called the Chief and a brilliant small-statured engineer named Mike, he fights to keep the launch on schedule. The novel mixes workshop detail with adventure, and it captures the early 1950s faith that spaceflight was near at hand.
25293-the-kirk-on-rutgers-farm:
Frederick Brückbauer's Kirk on Rutgers Farm, published in New York in 1919 with illustrations by Pauline Stone, tells the story of an old church at Market and Henry Streets. Its dedication honors the men and women who gave so that the church might remain amid a changing city.

Chapters recall Henry Rutgers, his mansion and tablet, the Nathan Hale statue, the first presidential mansion, and ministers such as Theodore Cuyler. Sunday school excursions by barge, with hymns on a melodeon, fill the memories, and Fanny Crosby's hymns were first sung in its primary class. The book is local history with affection.
25944-essentials-of-diseases-of-the-skin:
Henry W. Stelwagon prepares a question and answer manual on diseases of the skin, including the syphilodermata, for students of medicine. The book runs in the essentials style, with short prompts and terse replies meant for study and review. A seventh edition preface and a first edition preface frame the text, and an ad for Dorland's medical dictionary fronts the volume.

Sample entries ask how often skin troubles follow opium, quinine, or salicylic acid, and what forms they take. Opium brings rashes not uncommonly, quinine brings red and sometimes raised or spotted eruptions, often with peeling after. Stelwagon keeps each answer brief, clinical, and plain, a pocket guide for students facing skin disease on ward rounds.
25997-air-service-boys-flying-for-victor:
Charles Amory Beach sends the Air Service Boys over the Argonne in this 1920 tale of bombing the last German stronghold. Chapters open in action over the Argonne, with Yankee pluck, Jack's strange find, the story of the Lorraine waif, and a Red Cross nurse. Machine gun nests are cleaned out, the Red Triangle hut gives shelter, and a night raid tests the boys.

A frontispiece shows a plane shooting down at frightful speed. One scene finds Tom disgusted that a foe was shot in the leg just as Tom was set to jump him, robbing him of glory. Harry laughs it off, saying the main thing is that the desperate game is blocked. The book ends with the winning of the Argonne and a special selection for the boys.
26852-the-blue-germ:
Martin Swayne published this novel with Hodder and Stoughton in 1918. Its narrator, a doctor named Harden, trips over his black cat and strikes his forehead on the fender. He wakes after three days insensible with a clear idea in his mind. His colleague Wilfred Hammer calls the cat a wizard and the idea black magic, but Harden hurries back to his laboratory at St. Dane's Hospital to work. The chapters that follow bear titles like The Six Tubes, The Blue Disease, and Sarakoff's Manifesto.

The Sarakoff-Harden bacillus escapes into a lake, and a blue disease spreads whose victims show blue eyes and, stranger still, do not die. Later chapters trace first impressions of immortality, immortal love, a meeting at the Queen's Hall, and a revolt of the young. Swayne asks what a world does with death undone, and answers with murder, flight, and a great sleep.
26968-summer-snow-storm:
Adam Chase's comic science-fiction story starts with a forecast nobody believes: snow on the twenty-fifth of July. Weather Bureau Chief Botts rages at forecaster Johnny Sloman, whose sheet promises snow at eighty degrees, and the bureau's reputation for credulity hangs in the balance.

Then it actually snows, in summer, and Sloman, nursing a hangover and a lost fiancee, must face the weather he predicted by mistake. The story plays its impossible premise straight, wringing jokes from bureaucrats, managers, and a forecast that came true for all the wrong reasons.
27533-the-struggles-of-brown-jones-and-r:
One of the Firm wrote this comic novel of business life, edited by Anthony Trollope and published by Smith, Elder in London in 1870. It was reprinted from the Cornhill Magazine, with four illustrations, including a frontispiece of Jones vanquished by Mrs. Morony.

The chapters give the early histories of Mr. Brown and Mr. Robinson, and show how the partners selected their house of business. Nine times nine is eighty-one, the division of labour follows, and opening day arrives. Robinson walks on Blackfriars Bridge, the firm invents a new shirt, and Miss Brown pleads her own case. Trollope's editing keeps the comedy brisk.
28027-dwellers-in-arcady-the-story-of-an:
Albert Bigelow Paine's Dwellers in Arcady, published in March 1919, tells how he and his family took over a run-down farm and made it a home again. Paine, best known then for his life of Mark Twain, writes with humour about country neighbours, broken fences, and a cellar full of old stores. Thomas Fogarty supplied the pictures.

The chapters follow the work season by season: buying, mending, planting, and learning from farmers nearby. Paine treats the farm as a place to slow down and live simply, not as a business scheme. The book still reads as a warm, funny account of starting over in the country.
28586-prince-and-rover-of-cloverfield-fa:
Helen Fuller Orton's Prince and Rover of Cloverfield Farm, copyrighted in 1921 and published by Frederick A. Stokes, tells farm life through a horse and a dog. Farmer Hill buys a new horse because old Dan can no longer work fast or hard, and the children John, Sue, and Bobby watch him arrive. Prince the horse and Rover the dog then take turns at the center of each chapter.

Prince helps make bread and ice cream, brings home groceries, plays tag, and meets a supposed dragon. Rover gets cows out of the corn, brings them from pasture, rescues a little yellow chick, goes to church, and saves the house. The short chapters suit young readers, with farm work, humor, and small adventures throughout.
28652-bobby-of-cloverfield-farm:
Helen Fuller Orton wrote this children's book about a farm boy named Bobby, published in New York in 1922. Bobby lives on Cloverfield Farm, where his days follow the work and seasons of the place: sheep washing and shearing, haying, kite flying, and a horseback ride. His dog Rover and the farm animals share nearly every chapter, and pictures by R. Emmett Owen show the scenes.

Each chapter is a small, complete adventure, from a robin's return in spring to a rescue and a stormy night. The book suits young readers who like animals and country life, and it keeps its lessons light: Bobby forgets, makes mistakes, and learns by doing. It is a gentle portrait of farm childhood in the early twentieth century, told at a child's pace.
29269-a-succinct-view-of-the-importance-:
H. R. Hill published this pamphlet in London in 1845, arguing for a canal across the Panama isthmus. Hill threw his observations together after talking with gentlemen locally acquainted with the isthmus, who were astonished that science had realized so many undertakings of lesser utility while Panama waited.

Hill's case is twofold: importance and practicability. A canal would join oceans and shorten world trade, and the isthmus, he argues, allows it to be built. Writing decades before the canal opened, Hill speaks from the age of surveys and speculation. Readers get an early Victorian prospectus for Panama, short and confident, from before engineering and politics made the dream real.
29299-pirates-of-the-gorm:
Nat Schachner published this story in Astounding Stories in May 1932. Grant Pemberton wakes suddenly in his berth aboard a space-flier, every sense alert in deathly stillness. His hand slides under his pillow to his gun. A tiny scratching at the door, as if someone fumbled for the slide-switch, stops, and the panel moves slowly open.

Pemberton's trail, the magazine says, is the trail of vanished space ships, leading to a marvelous lake of fire. Pirates of the Gorm, as the title promises, haunt that trail. Readers get a pulp space adventure of pursuit and menace, opening in a dark cabin and moving toward a fiery, pirate-held place.
29303-operation-earthworm:
Joe Archibald wrote this rollicking science fiction story about Septimus Spink, the irrepressible hero who returns here. Spink, the magazine says, never bothered with Verne, since his own notions outdid even Verne's. Archibald, praised for versatility with the quill, tells the tale with slangy insouciance.

A news report dated circa 2022 from Interplanetary Press announces Spink, the first Earthman to visit New Mu and come back in a flying saucer. Uninvited, he crashes a meeting of leading cosmogonists at the University of Cincinnatus. Readers get a comic space tale, where a big, laughing hero juggles stars and planets and sends one tiny world spinning away.
29509-warm:
Robert Sheckley's short tale follows Anders, lying on his bed in his clothes, shoes and bow tie off, dreading the evening ahead. In twenty minutes he will pick up Judy, and he has just realized, seconds ago, that he is in love with her. He plans to propose, expects kisses, and pictures acceptance stamped across his forehead, figuratively speaking.

Anders gave voices no credence at all, until he heard them himself. Swiftly he listed the possibilities, starting with schizophrenia, as a joyous journey turns strange. Fans of Sheckley will enjoy a witty, unsettling tale about love, voices, and where a man winds up.
29598-four-little-blossoms-at-brookside-:
Mabel C. Hawley, author of Four Little Blossoms at Oak Hill School, wrote Four Little Blossoms at Brookside Farm, printed in 1920 by Saalfield of Akron and New York. It opens with a small girl, dark-eyed and rosy-cheeked, hurrying down a lawn with her doll. Chapters follow the rescue of Philip, an invitation, Aunt Polly, and the willing packers.

Dot's adventure, Brookside at last, the wreck of the raft, learning to milk, and lost in the woods follow, with Bobby crying that they must capture the ducks. The Blossoms learn farm life by doing it. Young readers and fans of series fiction will find a sunny, wholesome farm tale for children.
30291-kildares-of-storm:
Eleanor Mercein Kelly tells Kildares of Storm, published by the Century Company in New York in October 1916, with a frontispiece by Alonzo Kimball. Kelly dedicates the book to an unforgotten mother who moulded, for others than her daughter, the standard of great womanhood. An illustration shows Jacqueline of the eager lips turning her cheek, so that her mother's kiss should not disturb the memory of certain others.

A pleasant Kentucky road winds by nature's curves rather than art's, past a brook and through cool, leafy hollows, where a single-footing mare carries a woman cross-saddle. She holds a large china vase under one arm as the mare climbs a sudden little hill for a view over rolling country. An approaching automobile falls silent as its people stare, and she meets their gaze calmly.
30300-orphans-of-the-storm:
Henry MacMahon novelizes D. W. Griffith's motion picture epic on the immortal theme of the two orphans, in a Grosset and Dunlap volume from 1922, illustrated with scenes from the photo play. Lillian and Dorothy Gish, as the two orphans, front the book, and the story opens with two girls of Normandy, a journey to Paris, and what happened at the coach house. A fete at Bel-Air, the Frochards' den, tangled skeins, and the honor of the family follow.

Friends of the people, an attack on Danton, Louise before Notre Dame, and love as master of hearts lead to recognition, depths, and light rays in darkness. Revolution arrives, with prison delivery, a knife duel and escape, a new tyranny, and a pilgrim's adventures. The dread tribunal, vengeance come to judgment, the voice of Danton, and reprieve or agony follow. The novel gives Griffith's Revolution as a complete, swift story.
3034-the-anti-slavery-crusade-a-chronicl:
Jesse Macy wrote The Anti-Slavery Crusade, a chronicle of the gathering storm, for the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press in 1919. Contents run from the geography of the crusade and early crusaders through the turning point and the vindication of liberty. Later chapters cover the slavery issue in politics, the Underground Railroad, Bleeding Kansas, Charles Sumner, John Brown, and the Supreme Court in politics. Macy connects the Mexican War and Texas annexation to the crusade, noting that Lundy and Birney believed southern leaders planned to take Mexican territory to extend slavery.

Books as anti-slavery weapons get a chapter of their own. The volume gives a compact history of how abolition moved from moral protest to national crisis.
32344-pet-farm:
Roger Dee's tale, printed in Galaxy in February 1954, opens with Farrell fleeing toward the sheer face of a crater wall with a Falakian girl. She touches his arm and points back through scented, pearly mists at pursuers, stumbling over a half-forgotten Terran word. Farrell answers that they are too late, happy in the belief that what he did to the ship has made his new-found paradise secure.

Above them, a lacy network of bridging arches across the valley, vanishing into coloured mists, while the dusk deepens around the pair. Dee's title points to the alien paradise itself, a place that looks like heaven yet holds its captives fast. The story asks what freedom means when safety, comfort, and desire are supplied by someone else's world.
32610-the-long-arm:
Franz Habl tells of a man who returns to his Bavarian birthplace after thirty-five years abroad, poor in pocket and poorer in illusions. Working as an insurance agent, he shelters from rain in a coffee-house he knew as a boy, and meets Gustav, a school friend he had not seen in decades.

Gustav, once the best pupil in his class, tells a bitter tale of a harsh professor, a father's money, and a woman who bent his will. Habl lets the old friendship curdle into dread, as a past wrong reaches forward with a grasp that no distance can escape. The coffee-house scene is quiet at first. Dread builds slowly from talk, not from action.
33243-frying-pan-farm:
Elizabeth Brown Pryor's study traces Frying Pan Farm in Fairfax County, Virginia, through its long shift from working farm to historic site. Published by the county's planning office in September 1979, it divides the story into continuity and change, showing how land, buildings, and families held on through growth all around them. The text pairs a plain narrative with lists of pictures, notes, and sources for those who want more.

The farm's tale is told in two parts: first the thread that links its past to its present, then the forces that remade it. Pryor writes for local readers and visitors, not just scholars, and her account helps explain why a patch of farm life survived in a busy county. It is a clear, useful guide to one place and to the wider story of Fairfax land use.
34072-the-evolution-of-an-empire-a-brief:
Mary Parmele wrote this brief historical sketch of Germany, in a second edition published in New York. Chapters run from Indo-European migrations and the divisions of the Aryan family through Hermann, Ulfila, the fall of Rome before Alaric, and the Anglo-Saxon occupation of Britain. Clovis, Charlemagne, and the growth of church power follow.

Later chapters treat the Thirty Years' War, Napoleon, Waterloo, Bismarck and Koniggratz, and William crowned German emperor at Versailles. Parmele writes for general readers in short, clear chapters. The book offers a compact history of Germany from tribe to empire.
4590-after-the-storm:
T. S. Arthur published After the Storm at Philadelphia in 1868, opening with a June day and a chapter called The War of the Elements. Lovers meet under a cloud, and the storm bursts. The book follows what comes after: a letter, a flight and return, and a reconciliation. Then come a new acquaintance, bonds, reformers, and a startling experience. Later chapters speak of captivity, weariness, and shipwrecked life, before turning to a ministering angel and love that never dies.

Arthur uses storm weather as a picture of passion, error, and repentance, in the moral style of his day. His characters fall, reform, and are tested again, and the book argues that a life can be remade after damage. Readers get a long, earnest domestic novel about marriage, temptation, and second chances, written for a nineteenth-century audience that liked its lessons plain and its endings hard-won.
498-rebecca-of-sunnybrook-farm:
Kate Douglas Wiggin follows Rebecca Randall, a bright farm girl sent to live with strict aunts in Riverboro, in this beloved novel. Rebecca arrives by stage coach in a buff calico dress, full of talk, dreams, and pluck. School, chores, and town folk test her, yet her spirit lifts the whole house.

Wiggin writes with humor and warmth, tracking Rebecca from seven sisters at Sunnybrook to a young woman of grace. Aunts Miranda and Jane, friends, and a banquet lamp mark her growth. The book endures as a classic of girlhood, where imagination and kind grit win a hard home's love.
6006-under-the-storm:
Charlotte M. Yonge tells of Steadfast's charge during England's mid-seventeenth-century civil wars, when Englishmen fought one another and quiet homes became sanctuaries. The chapters promise a trust, stragglers, kirk rapine, desolation, and a hermit's gulley, with wintry times and a terrible harvest day.

Stead in possession, farewell to the Cavaliers, Godly Venn's troop, and the assault of the cavern follow, with Emlyn's service and troth at the heart of the tale. Yonge writes of loyalty kept under pressure. The novel asks what steadfastness costs when war divides neighbors and kin.
7302-my-friends-at-brook-farm:
John Van Der Zee Sears recalls Brook Farm in chapters on the old colonie, friend Greeley, and a stranger in a strange land. A bad beginning and a good ending, entertainments, the school, oddments, and Fourier and the farmers follow. Horace Greeley, Ralph Waldo Emerson, Charles A. Dana, and Nathaniel Hawthorne appear among the illustrations, with the Hive and a pioneer kindergarten beside them.

Sears dedicates the book to Joseph Hornor Coates of Philadelphia and writes as one who lived inside the experiment, not as a distant historian. His memories mix comedy, idealism, and plain farm work, showing a utopian community in daily dress. The book keeps Brook Farm human, fond, and a little rueful.
8716-the-strong-arm:
Robert Barr sets The Strong Arm in a world of outlaws, emperors, and secret courts, opening with the beautiful jailer of Gudenfels. The aged Emir Soldan sits in his tent, smiling the crafty smile of an experienced man, aware that rebellion brews among his young commanders. Later chapters promise the revenge of the outlaw, a city of fear, the peril of the emperor, the needle dagger, and the holy Fehm, the secret tribunal of medieval Germany.

Further episodes include the count's apology, a conversion, an invitation, the archbishop's gift, Count Konrad's courtship, the long ladder, and the warrior maid of San Carlos, with ambassadors' pigeons carrying secrets. Barr mixes romance, adventure, and intrigue with a journalist's pace. Readers who enjoy historical swashbucklers will find a rousing, if fanciful, tour of castles, camps, and conspiracies.
adopting-an-abandoned-farm: Kate Sanborn adopts an abandoned farm in this 1891 volume, running from Gotham to Gooseville through auctions, buying a horse, pets, a poultry farm, ghosts, and daily distractions. The prose of New England farm life, the passing of the peacocks, and a looking back close the account. Weary of boarding at seashore and mountain and hating hotel life, she visited a country friend at Gooseville, Connecticut. Gooseville is an assumed name for Foxboro, Massachusetts, where she passed three happy weeks.
after-the-storm:
T. S. Arthur's After the Storm, published in Philadelphia in 1868, is a domestic novel of marriage under strain. A June tempest, described at operatic length, opens the book. The storm figures the lovers' coming troubles: a cloud, a sign, and a bursting follow in the chapter titles. Two proud young people marry with the weather already changing.

Chapters move through bonds, reformers, and a startling experience. The wife grows weary of constraint, and an irrevocable decree parts the pair. A shipwrecked life and a palsied heart mark the middle years. A ministering angel and the assurance that love never dies prepare the close. Arthur, the temperance moralist, here warns against pride and haste in marriage. The storm of his title is weather between two hearts, and its effects linger.
britannica-1911-barm: Barm is a word common to the Teutonic languages, and this short 1911 Britannica entry gives its two related uses in brewing and baking. It names the scum that forms on the top of malt liquor while the liquor is fermenting. It also names yeast itself: the yeast used to leaven bread, raising the dough, and the yeast set into liquor to start fermentation there.
britannica-1911-berm:
Berm, probably a variant of the word brim, is a narrow ledge of ground, generally the level bank of a river. This very short 1911 Britannica entry gives the term in two settings, one drawn from Egypt and one from military works, and supports each with a named source.

In Egypt the whole area reached by the Nile is included in the berm. Near Berber, a report on the Upper Nile of 1904, quoted here, describes a well-marked alluvial berm of recent formation, varying in width up to perhaps a couple of kilometres. In military language the berm is the space of ground between the base of a rampart and the ditch.
britannica-1911-brook-farm:
Brook Farm was the name of a tract of land in West Roxbury, Massachusetts, where from 1841 to 1847 a communistic experiment was tried and failed. It grew out of New England Transcendentalism, though many leading transcendentalists took no direct part. George Ripley started the project and in effect directed it throughout its six years.

Ripley's own words set the aim. Thinker and worker were to be joined in the same person. All were to get work fitted to their tastes and talents, and the fruits of their industry. Menial service was to end by opening education and profit to all. So to build a society of free, cultivated people living simply. In short, the best conditions for an ideal civilisation with labour cut to a minimum. The long entry tests that high aim against the farm's actual life and failure.
bunny-brown-and-his-sister-sue-on-grandp:
Laura Lee Hope wrote a Bunny Brown tale of a farm stay, put out by Grosset and Dunlap. Florence England Nosworthy drew the plates. A letter from Grandpa heads the chapter list. Mother calls in vain from the porch in the first scene. Sue comes round the house with her doll in one arm.

A runaway monkey and a big automobile shake the early run. A queer slide and the start for the farm come next. Gypsy-style road life and a woodland camp fill the heart. A night scare marks the late turns. Farm work and farm play at child scale form the stock. The front list shows this as an early book in the Brown line, with just four kin tales in print at its back. Hope's soft frame — home love, small fright, safe end — holds firm.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-form:
Form is a key word in philosophy, from the Greek eidos and the Latin forma, first meaning shape or outward look, then kind or nature. Plato used it for kind, while Aristotle made it the inner principle that makes a thing what it is, its essence. The entry sorts the uses carefully: substantial form gives matter its specific nature, accidental form gives it qualities like size or colour. A separated form, like the human soul, exists apart from matter.

Later thinkers get their turn, from Kant's forms of intuition, space and time, and forms of thought. Theological uses of the word include the form of words in a dogma and the sacramental form that makes a rite effective. Readers who want the scholastic vocabulary straight will find each sense defined and traced to its source, with Aristotle at the centre of the whole account.
child-of-storm:
H Rider Haggard's Child of Storm returns Allan Quatermain to Zululand. In chapter one he hears of Mameena. She is a beautiful, ambitious girl, called a child of storm for the tempest born with her. The dwarf Zikali, wisest and most sinister of witch-doctors, brews moonshine plots against the Zulu royal house. A buffalo with a cleft horn opens the hunting.

Mameena marries Saduko, who brings the marriage gift of cattle, while loving and scheming toward princes; King Panda's sons Umbelazi and Cetewayo move toward civil war. Saduko shrugs that nothing is quite perfect in the world when her love is questioned. Haggard knew Zululand firsthand, and Mameena stands among his most fully imagined African characters.
doe-osti-2588594-emosaic-electrification:
James Stoupis of ABB Inc. led this final report for award DE-EE0009194 on eMosaic, a platform for grid-informed smart charging of electric transit buses. Rocky Mountain Power and Utah State University were team members, and Utah Transit Authority depots anchor the deployment.

Charging a bus fleet is a grid problem as much as a transport one. eMosaic coordinates the chargers, Level 2 units plus 300-kilowatt pantograph and DC fast chargers, through open protocols. OCPP 1.6 speaks to the chargers, and OpenADR 2.0b carries grid signals. A learning agent and a price generator sit in the platform, with a grid health simulator and a bus planner around them. The report is candid about data pain. Raw operating records for the Ogden routes had to be inspected by hand. Buses were missing data or sitting at the depot all day. Only after that cleanup could route discharge patterns be modeled.
doe-osti-3000537-first-order-transport-o:
Stephen Brooks of Brookhaven National Laboratory works out beam mathematics in technical note BNL-229092-2025-TECH, also numbered CA/AP/726, dated 24 October 2025. Accelerator designers track a bunch of charged particles as it travels through magnets. Brooks treats the bunch as a cold, uniform ellipsoid: a football-shaped cloud, evenly filled, whose particles share one orderly motion pattern rather than random thermal jitter.

The whole cloud is captured by a 21-element vector. Six elements fix its centre in position and momentum, six more give its shape through a covariance matrix, and nine describe how velocity varies across it. From that compact description, the note derives first-order transport: how each element evolves, step by step, as the ellipsoid passes through beamline elements. Linear maps of this kind are the workhorse of lattice design, letting engineers predict bunch shape at every point without simulating millions of particles.
doe-osti-3001267-status-report-on-design:
Sven Vogel, Bjørn Clausen and Charles Hill of Los Alamos report design progress in LA-UR-25-30773, issued 30 October 2025, on a rig that will cook and squeeze nuclear fuel while neutrons watch. Fuel inside a reactor endures heat and stress that reshape its microstructure. Models predict the response, but licensing new fuels needs experimental proof. Most rod deformation sits in the cladding. Yet the fuel's creep, swelling and cracking at operating and accident temperatures still matters.

The plan uses neutron diffraction at LANSCE, the Los Alamos neutron source. It reads crystal structure, phase changes and defect densities inside a sample under load. Dislocation driven peak broadening tracks how deformation builds up. The status report sets out the in situ test: furnace, load frame and diffraction geometry, and how it will verify deformation models. It is a design stage document, laying instrument groundwork for experiments to come.
doe-osti-3018134-crada-number-nfe-22-093:
Alex Stiles of Oak Ridge National Laboratory wrote this November 2025 CRADA final report, ORNL/TM-2025/4394, for agreement NFE-22-09375 with Vitriform3D Inc. The project printed with household glass waste. Stiles, a participant in the laboratory's LEEP entrepreneurship program, used an Innovent binder jetting system to print recycled glass with a PEI binder system first developed at the laboratory.

Flexural testing, bending samples until they fail, was the primary check on formulation improvements. The work proposed a new additive method that turns a waste stream every town has into printable feedstock. Larger-scale prints were planned to test how the composite powder and binder behave in a real manufacturing setting. Printed tools from the project were to be evaluated in processes such as compression molding. The report closes a first loop: waste glass in, testable parts out, with commercialization possibilities and future collaboration plans stated.
doe-osti-3021680-watching-the-watchers-w:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory abbreviated final report LLNL-TR-2016525, by Matthew Sottile, dated March 2026, closes LDRD project 23-ERD-024, 'Watching the Watchers.' The title states the problem: laboratories rely on software tools to vouch for the safety of other things, so who vouches for the tools? The project tested formal reasoning methods for building assurance cases about the assurance software itself.

Demonstrator projects applied the methods to use cases drawn from Livermore's mission work, with additive manufacturing as the key focus, examining the workflow from design file to finished part. Artificial intelligence, data analysis, and concurrent programming tools were also explored. The team identified viable methods at different levels of rigor, difficulty, and scalability. Follow-on research is planned to adapt the prototypes to mission applications, including analysis of manufactured parts before, during, and after fabrication.
doe-osti-3029250-ultrasep-acoustic-separ: Particles getting sorted by sound waves got their DOE acoustic platform, and this UltraSep separates the mix. The pages detail the results. The engineers get their data. The platform was separation. The mix were separates. The waves were sound. The sorting were particles.

doe-osti-3364152-agr-5-6-7-thermal-model: AGR-5/6/7 got gap-modeled, and this DOE thermal model covers non-uniform. The pages detail the gas findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The gaps were gas. The data were nuclear. The 5/6/7 were AGR. The uniform were non. The nuclear were folks.
doe-osti-3375596-scientific-discovery-wi: Machine learning can find patterns, but it often ignores the laws of physics. Robert Stephany's report explores physics-informed system identification — teaching algorithms to respect physical laws while discovering how systems behave. The result is AI that learns real science, not just statistics.
doe-osti-3376270-chlorine-isotope-separa: Chlorine got isotope-separated, and this DOE text covers thermal diffusion. The pages detail the separations findings. The physicists get their data. The diffusion was thermal. The data were physicist. The chlorine were separations. The physicists were data. The diffusion were thermal.
doe-osti-3377976-preparation-of-iodine-b: Iodine waste got HIP-pressed, and this DOE text covers hot isostatic forms. The pages detail the preparation findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The forms were waste. The data were nuclear. The pressing were isostatic. The hot were forms.
doe-osti-3382495-inl-crmo-xrf-special-re: INL CRMO got XRF-calibrated, and this DOE special report No.3 covers ceramics. The pages detail the methods findings. The engineers get their data. The analysis was brick. The data were engineer. The No.3 were special. The brick were ceramics.
doe-osti-3383526-data-life-cycle-livewir: Livewire got data-life-cycled, and this DOE text covers the platform. The pages detail the cycle findings. The computing folks get their data. The platform was data. The data were computing. The cycle were life. The platform were data.
doe-osti-3395430-sem-ebsd-characterizati: Baffle bolts got SEM-characterized, and this DOE text covers EBSD microscopy. The pages detail the former findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The studies were X-ray. The data were nuclear. The former were baffle. The microscopy were high energy.
doe-osti-3412006-inl-crmo-xrf-special-re: Obsidian tools carry a chemical fingerprint of the volcano they came from. This INL special report details how to calibrate XRF instruments — which read that fingerprint with X-rays — for studying obsidian artifacts. Good calibration lets archaeologists trace ancient trade routes stone by stone.
doe-osti-3412008-inl-crmo-xrf-special-re: Non-obsidian got XRF-calibrated, and this DOE special covers fine-grained analysis. The pages detail the No.2 findings. The researchers get their data. The methods were calibration. The data were researcher. The grained were fine. The calibration were methods.

The efficient was highly. The data were energy. The planar were perovskite. The pressed were thermally.
doe-osti-3874816-review-of-metrics-for-w: Wind models got metric-reviewed, and this DOE review covers performance evaluation. The pages detail the review findings. The energy folks get their data. The metrics were performance. The data were energy. The evaluation were performance. The wind were review.
fishing-with-a-worm:
Perry defends the lowly worm in Fishing with a Worm, printed in 1916. Bliss Perry takes his text from Izaak Walton: the last fish I caught was with a worm. His essay is a fond brief for the plain angler. The born fisherman, he says, is a pattern of inconsistency, and a defective logic is his portion.

The sampled pages grant the fly its due with grace. The artificial fly, Perry writes, is the poetry of angling: light as thistle-down, it falls where you will it, and sings like a violin string when the leader tightens. Yet his case is for the worm and for the series of single trout that lurk, each one, under a log or in a ripple. The book is a short, witty essay on the philosophy of fishing, not a manual of knots and baits.
govdocs-archive_org-the-sacred-proto-wri: Herman Wirth devoted his career to the search for mankind's oldest writing. The Sacred Proto-Writing of Mankind studies early signs and argues for runic origins behind them. Wirth read scratches and symbols as the remains of one sacred script from the far north. His methods were doubted even in his own time. The volume serves readers of runic studies and of the scholars who built grand systems on small marks.
kit-of-greenacre-farm:
Izola Forrester's Kit of Greenacre Farm is a novel published in 1919. Its contents promise farm scenes, family debate, and some playful mystery. Chapter titles mention a sign of the mummy and royal mummies.

Kit appears in chapter after chapter as the family's lively center. One chapter says Kit rises to prophesy, and another says Kit locates a founder. A dean and his outposts also figure in the story. Young readers of its day got a bright farm tale with secrets mixed in. School and college figures appear in chapter titles like the dean's outposts. The mix of farm life and campus life widens the tale.
lair-of-the-white-worm:
Bram Stoker wrote this last novel of his life, and it came out in 1911, a year before his death. He set it in his wife's home shire, in the north of England. The tale draws on a local legend of a great white worm that plagued the land.

A young man comes home to find a strange, cold feud round two old houses. Lady Arabella, one of the foes, hides a dread link to the worm of the old tale. Weird and hot with dread, the book is the most strange of all Stoker's works.
my-friends-at-brook-farm:
John Van der Zee Sears recalls his days at Brook Farm, the famed commune. Portraits in the book show Greeley, Emerson, Dana, and Hawthorne. Chapters treat the school, fun nights, and Fourier's strange plan. One is called A Stranger in a Strange Land.

Sears opens with Dutch settlers on the Hudson in 1624. That long view frames the farm's bold hopes. V1 calls the book a warm, firsthand memoir of the experiment. Thinkers there dreamed of a fairer way to live and work. Sears writes of friends, not theories, which keeps the dream human and the failure gentle.
nasa-tm-19680000583-electron-microscopy-:
Bruno C. Buzek, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, developed a way to peek inside a metal powder before it is pressed into a part. Powder blends mix hard oxide particles, the dispersoid, into metal powder. Where those particles sit at the start shapes the finished product.

Buzek's technique wraps the blend in a thin carbon skin, then leaches the metal away. The leftover oxide particles show their size and clumping, unobstructed by metal. He tried it on nickel, tungsten, chromium, and nichrome blended with thoria or alumina. Well-spread particles stayed well spread after sintering; early clusters survived as large particles.
nasa-tm-19700033263-direct-near-identity:
David P. Stern of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in October 1970. It treats direct near-identity canonical transformations, a tool of mathematical physics. Such transformations restate a problem in new variables that sit close to the old ones, which can make hard orbit equations easier to handle.

Stern presents what he calls a somewhat new approach to this old subject. He writes the transformation as a series built on a small parameter, order by order. The rules each order must obey are tied to a generating function and its gradients. Some choices of form match the conventional version, and others match Lie's form, he notes. Properties and uses of the representation close the discussion.
nasa-tm-19720008341-cold-startup-and-low:
James E Vrancik and Richard C Bainbridge of the Lewis Research Center reported cold weather tests in December 1971, as NASA TM X-67995. The hardware was the full electrical subsystem of the Brayton cycle power system. It included the inverter, a motor driven pump, and the direct current supply. Speed control gear and the main control system joined the test as well. Space hardware must wake up and run in deep cold.

The parts sat on cold plates inside a vacuum chamber. Tests covered a range from room temperature down to fifty degrees below zero Celsius. Startup trials ran alongside steady cold performance checks. No failures occurred during the whole series. The team found no sign of trouble for safe Brayton operation.
ostrovsky-the-storm:
Katerina, trapped in a loveless marriage under a tyrannical mother-in-law, reaches for love and is destroyed in Ostrovsky's The Storm, in English. A thunderstorm breaks over her Volga town as her inner tempest breaks into confession. The play, from 1859, became Russia's great tragedy of a woman's revolt against the dark kingdom of merchant patriarchy.

Katerina's longing for freedom is phrased like prayer and poetry, set against the Kabanovs' airless household. Her lover is too weak, her world too strong, and the river waits below the cliff. The drama inspired Janacek's opera Katya Kabanova, carrying her story across Europe. Russian audiences have wept over Katerina for over a century and a half. The Storm remains Ostrovsky's summit.
podcast-dannyjones-piDqTbBwWRM:
Former housing official Catherine Fitts joins Danny Jones to claim that twenty-one trillion dollars in black budget funds a rogue breakaway civilization. Fitts once served in the US housing agency. She has tracked missing state funds for years.

Fitts explains how she found the gaps in the books and where she thinks the cash went. She argues a hidden group now lives off the grid with tech far past ours. Jones asks what proof can be shown in the open. Listeners get her full case at length. The library files the talk as an archive record of her claims.
rebecca-of-sunnybrook-farm:
Kate Douglas Wiggin's novel follows a girl named Rebecca through twenty-eight chapters, and Wiggin dedicated the book to her mother. A verse from Wordsworth stands at the front, praising a dancing shape drawn from May-time and dawn. The chapter list names Riverboro as the place where much of the story unfolds.

Early chapters treat Rebecca's relations, her point of view, and secrets in Riverboro. Mr. Aladdin enters midway, with a banquet lamp, seasons of growth, and gray days and gold. Later titles speak of a change of heart, clover blossoms, roses of joy, and a sky line that widens. The close is named for an old phrase, the inevitable yoke.
that-old-time-child-roberta-her-home-lif:
Sophie Fox Sea wrote That Old-Time Child, Roberta, subtitled Her Home-Life on the Farm, printed at Louisville by John P. Morton and Company in 1892. Sea gave the child's tale to her friend Mrs. Preston Pope, whose love of children first sparked it.

Roberta Marsden, called Lil Missus by the Black folk of the place, lives on a Kentucky farm in the years just before the Civil War. She is drawn as a lovely child in a warm, busy home. Readers get a fond, detailed look at old-time Southern farm life through a girl's eyes, with games, kin, servants, and seasons recalled as a lost world worth saving on the page.
the-anti-slavery-crusade-a-chronicle-of-: Contents alone map Jesse Macy's The Anti-Slavery Crusade, a chronicle of the gathering storm printed by Yale University Press in 1919. Early chapters set the ground and name the first crusaders, then reach a turning point and a vindication of liberty. Politics takes over next: the slavery issue in public life and the passing of the Whig Party. Later chapters treat the Underground Railroad, books as weapons against slavery, Bleeding Kansas, Charles Sumner, President Buchanan, the Supreme Court, and John Brown, with a note on books at the end.
the-fat-of-the-land-the-story-of-an-amer:
John Williams Streeter wrote The Fat of the Land as the story of an American farm, printed at New York in 1904. He gives the book to Polly, and the early chapters tell why he wrote it and how he hunted for land.

Streeter tells of the first visit to the farm and the work of making it pay. A city man turned farmer, he set down costs, crops, stock, and the slow gains of skill. Such farm tales were a school for town folk dreaming of land. His plain aim was to show that a farm could yield both a living and a life.
the-mystery-of-monastery-farm:
H. R. Naylor's 1908 novel The Mystery of Monastery Farm opens with Chapter I, A Great Bank Robbery. In a year left blank, April the eleventh is when the Bank of England's officers receive notice of a special meeting at ten that night. Fifteen directors take their places, joined unusually by two paying tellers and by Major Andrews, chief of the Bow Street detective service, with two assistants.

The cashier, Mr. Bone, states the cause plainly: a large amount of currency has been taken from the paying teller's room. Senior teller Mr. Roe explains that at nine that morning he brought currency from the vault and set it on a side table. At two o'clock, when he needed it, the package was gone, without the faintest clue.
the-story-of-an-african-farm:
Olive Schreiner opens this South African novel with a preface. She also wrote under the name Ralph Iron. She thanks the public and critics. They received a little book far removed from English daily life. She explains a puzzle readers had raised: two strangers appear in the story, and the second is not the first returning in a new guise as husband or lover.

Schreiner contrasts two ways of painting human life. The stage method marshals every character. It tickets each one, who reappears at the right crisis. The method of real life works otherwise. People come, act on each other, and pass away. No one can predict them. She also refuses the wild adventure some critics wanted, noting that such books are best written far from the facts among which she grew up.
the-strong-arm:
Robert Barr opens this collection of historical tales with one chapter. It is called The Beautiful Jailer of Gudenfels. A contents list promises more. A city of fear and the peril of the emperor lead off. A needle dagger and the Holy Fehm follow. Stories such as The Count's Apology appear too. The Long Ladder and The Warrior Maid of San Carlos close the heads.

The aged Emir Soldan sits in his tent. He smiles the crafty smile of an experienced man. He knows rebellion is brewing among his young commanders. They think him grown too old for the fray. Unbelievers have set foot on the sacred soil of Syria. The Emir has counselled coolness and prudence. He would not dash against the German leader. Impatience is breaking his camp apart. He gathers the young men to address them.
the-wrack-of-the-storm: Maurice Maeterlinck's The Wrack of the Storm appears here only in a list of his works. That list divides his books into essays and plays. Essays named include The Life of the Bee and The Buried Temple. The Treasure of the Humble also appears. Sister Beatrice is named among the plays. No essay text from The Wrack of the Storm itself follows in the pages present in this record.
under-the-storm: Charlotte M. Yonge wrote Under the Storm, also titled Steadfast's Charge. The pages here hold the title page and a contents list of sixteen chapters, and the story itself is not shown. Chapter names point to England's civil war years: a trust given, stragglers, desolation, wintry times, a farewell to the Cavaliers, and a troop led by Godly Venn. One late chapter promises a table of love in the wilderness, and the last visible title is a fair offer.
wildflowers-of-the-farm:
Arthur O. Cooke wrote Flowers of the Farm for the Country-Life Readers series. The contents promise walks in a coppice, flowers on walls, clover, and hay-field and corn-field chapters. Chapter two begins outside Willow Farm, by a broad curving gravel drive. A white gate opens to the lane, and a strip of flowers and shrubs lines the drive.

An old mulberry tree stands by the front door, and a lawn and vegetable garden lie beyond. A small nut coppice waits past the garden for a March morning walk. Yellow primroses brighten a sunny bank along the way. Cooke teaches farm flowers through a child's walk, in plain and friendly terms.
